whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the B2C Commerce Architect exam for?

personas.label: Senior SFCC architects
personas.description: You have led B2C Commerce builds and want proof that you can design whole storefront programmes, not just features.

personas.label: Technical leads evaluating commerce patterns
personas.description: You decide between SFRA and a headless storefront, and you plan integrations, caching and site operations.

personas.label: Solution architects
personas.description: You work on retail projects where B2C Commerce has to fit with Order Management, Marketing Cloud and outside systems.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the B2C Commerce Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is one of the harder commerce exams. You need deep B2C Commerce knowledge and you have to weigh trade-offs, such as speed versus flexibility or custom code versus standard features. Salesforce lists B2C Commerce Developer as a prerequisite.
bullets: 60 scored multiple-choice questions, plus a few unscored ones, in about 105 minutes.
About 63% to pass, about 38 correct answers out of 60. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book, since Salesforce updates these.
Trade-off questions. SFRA or headless, OCAPI or SCAPI, page caching choices, and how to integrate with other systems.
Experience matters. Years on real B2C Commerce projects, with different traffic levels and site setups, is the best preparation.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People who have taken a site live and supported it during peak trading do best. Before you book, aim for 75% or more on practice tests and be able to explain why you would pick a headless storefront or not.

examFormat.heading: B2C Commerce Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions are scenarios. A typical one describes a retailer with several brands and countries and asks for the best way to set up sites, catalogs, code or integrations.
bestWayToPass: Know the cartridge path: Cartridges on the left override those on the right. Keep custom code in your own cartridges, not in the base.
Understand caching: Page caching is the main lever for speed. Know what can be cached and what must stay dynamic.
Learn the APIs: SCAPI and the Shopper APIs for new headless builds, OCAPI for older ones, and SLAS for shopper login.
Plan multi-site setups: Shared master catalog, separate storefront catalogs, price books and locales per site.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design and run Salesforce B2C Commerce sites: choosing a storefront approach, setting up sites and catalogs, planning integrations, and keeping sites fast and secure.

keyConcepts.h2: B2C Commerce Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Architecture Patterns & Scalability
blocks.body: A B2C Commerce realm holds several instances: sandboxes for developers, then Development, Staging and Production. Code and data are built and tested on Staging, then **replicated** to Production. A realm can run many sites, which share code but can have their own catalogs, prices and settings. For a retailer with several brands or countries, the usual design is one **master catalog** for products, separate **storefront catalogs** per site to control what each one shows, and separate **price books** per currency or market. Scale comes from the platform, but your code must still be efficient: avoid heavy logic on every page request and use jobs for batch work.

blocks.heading: Storefront Architecture & Headless Commerce
blocks.body: **SFRA** (Storefront Reference Architecture) is the standard server-rendered storefront. You customise it by adding your own cartridges on top, without editing the base code. **Composable Storefront** (PWA Kit with Managed Runtime) is the headless option: a React front end that calls the B2C Commerce APIs. Headless gives more freedom in the front end and fits teams with strong JavaScript skills, but it means more to build and run yourself. Pick SFRA when speed to market and standard features matter most, and headless when the brand needs a very custom experience or one front end for several back ends.

blocks.heading: Integration Architecture: OCAPI, SCAPI & Connectors
blocks.body: **SCAPI** (Salesforce Commerce API), including the Shopper APIs, is the modern API set and is the default for new headless builds. **OCAPI** (Open Commerce API) is the older API, still used on many sites. **SLAS** handles shopper login and tokens for headless storefronts. For outside systems, use **service framework** definitions in Business Manager so calls have timeouts, logging and circuit breakers. Large data such as product feeds and inventory usually come in through scheduled **jobs** that import XML or CSV files. Payment, tax and address providers usually plug in through certified **LINK cartridges**.

blocks.heading: Performance, Caching & CDN Strategy
blocks.body: Page caching is the biggest performance lever. Cache whole pages or page parts with the iscache tag, and keep user-specific bits, like the mini cart, as small uncached includes loaded separately. Set sensible cache times and clear the cache when catalog or content changes. The **eCDN** serves images and static files from locations close to the shopper. Watch the platform **quotas**, which limit things like the number of objects or API calls per request, and fix code that breaks them before peak season. Test with realistic traffic before big sale days.

blocks.heading: Security, Compliance & Site Operations
blocks.body: Never store raw card numbers on the platform. Use a payment provider's cartridge so card data goes straight to them as a token, which keeps you out of most PCI scope. Use role-based access in Business Manager so each team only sees what it needs. Handle shopper privacy requests, consent and cookie rules for each country. For operations, plan code deployments through Staging with replication, schedule jobs outside peak hours, and set up log monitoring and alerts. Have a clear plan for peak trading such as Black Friday, including code freezes.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce B2C Commerce Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions describe a retailer's needs and ask for the best design. Look for clues about how many brands and countries there are, how custom the front end must be, and how much traffic to expect.

blocks.heading: SFCC Architecture & Multi-Site
blocks.body: Several brands or countries usually means one realm, several sites, a shared master catalog and separate storefront catalogs and price books.

blocks.heading: Cartridge Architecture
blocks.body: Put custom code in your own cartridges and place them to the left of the base on the cartridge path. Never edit the base cartridge directly.

blocks.heading: Performance Optimization
blocks.body: Cache as much of each page as you can. Load shopper-specific parts separately so they don't stop the rest of the page being cached.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns
blocks.body: SCAPI for new headless builds, jobs for large feeds, the service framework for outside calls, and LINK cartridges for payment and tax.

blocks.heading: Security Architecture
blocks.body: Tokenise payments through a provider, give Business Manager users only the roles they need, and respect each country's privacy rules.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After B2C Commerce Architect, many people move toward the wider architect credentials:

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer runs three brands in five countries. Most products are shared, but each brand shows a different range and each country has its own prices. What is the best catalog design?
options: One master catalog, storefront catalogs, price books
Store the prices as custom attributes on each of the products
A separate master catalog for every site
One storefront catalog shared by all sites
sampleQuestions.explanation: A shared master catalog avoids duplicating products. Storefront catalogs control what each site shows, and price books handle prices per market.
whyWrong: Prices in custom attributes skip the price book system and are hard to manage.
Separate master catalogs duplicate shared products and make updates harder.
One shared storefront catalog can't show a different range per brand.

sampleQuestions.question: A developer needs to change how the checkout page works on an SFRA site. Where should the change go?
options: In Business Manager site preferences
In a custom cartridge earlier on the cartridge path
In a cartridge placed to the right of the base cartridge
Directly in the app_storefront_base cartridge
sampleQuestions.explanation: Cartridges on the left override those on the right. Putting changes in your own cartridge keeps the base untouched, so upgrades are easier.
whyWrong: Site preferences change settings, not page logic.
A cartridge on the right is overridden by the base, so the change wouldn't apply.
Editing the base makes future SFRA upgrades painful.

sampleQuestions.question: A brand wants a highly custom, app-like front end built by their React team, with fast page loads. Which approach fits best?
options: OCAPI calls from ISML templates
SFRA with a custom theme
Composable Storefront on the Commerce APIs
Business Manager content slots and nothing more
sampleQuestions.explanation: Composable Storefront is the headless option built on React and the Commerce APIs, and it suits teams that want full control of the front end.
whyWrong: ISML is SFRA's template language. Calling OCAPI from it isn't a headless design.
SFRA is server-rendered and less suited to an app-like React experience.
Content slots manage content, not the whole front-end design.

sampleQuestions.question: Category pages load slowly at peak. Each page includes the shopper's mini cart. What should the architect recommend?
options: Move the whole category page into a job
Turn off page caching to keep the cart accurate
Add more product images
Cache the page, load the mini cart uncached
sampleQuestions.explanation: Caching the main page and loading the shopper-specific mini cart separately gives fast pages without showing the wrong cart.
whyWrong: Jobs run in the background and can't serve live pages.
Turning off caching makes the slowdown worse.
More images slow the page further.

sampleQuestions.question: A new headless storefront needs shoppers to log in and get tokens to call the Shopper APIs. What should be used?
options: Shopper Login and API Access Service
Business Manager user accounts
A shared API key in the front end
Basic authentication applied on every single call
sampleQuestions.explanation: SLAS is the service for shopper login and API tokens in headless B2C Commerce builds.
whyWrong: Business Manager accounts are for staff, not shoppers.
A shared key in the front end can be copied by anyone.
Basic auth isn't how the Shopper APIs authenticate shoppers.

sampleQuestions.question: The retailer must avoid storing card numbers on the platform to reduce PCI scope. What is the right design?
options: A provider LINK cartridge that tokenises
Encrypt the card numbers inside a custom object
Email card details to the finance team
Store cards in session data only
sampleQuestions.explanation: With tokenisation, the card data goes to the payment provider and the site only keeps a token, which greatly reduces PCI scope.
whyWrong: Encrypted cards on the platform still bring the site into PCI scope.
Emailing card details is insecure and breaks PCI rules.
Session data still passes through and stores card data.

sampleQuestions.question: Inventory levels for 500,000 products arrive from the warehouse system every hour. How should they be loaded?
options: One OCAPI call per product every hour
Updating stock during each page view
Manual updates in Business Manager
A scheduled inventory import job
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scheduled jobs that import inventory files are the standard way to handle large, regular feeds.
whyWrong: Half a million API calls per hour is wasteful and may hit quotas.
Updating stock on page views slows pages and doesn't keep stock in sync.
Manual updates can't keep up at this scale.

sampleQuestions.question: Code has been tested on Staging and is ready for Production. How does it usually reach Production?
options: Developers upload it straight to Production from their sandboxes
Replication from Staging to Production
Rebuilding the site by hand
Copying files by FTP
sampleQuestions.explanation: Code and data are prepared on Staging and then replicated to Production, which keeps the two in step.
whyWrong: Uploading straight to Production skips testing and is not the standard flow.
Rebuilding by hand is slow and error-prone.
FTP isn't how code is deployed to Production.

sampleQuestions.question: A call to an outside tax service sometimes hangs and slows checkout. What should the architect use for this call?
options: Running the call in a nightly job
The service framework with a timeout and circuit breaker
A plain HTTP call with no timeout
Calling the tax service directly from the shopper's own browser
sampleQuestions.explanation: Service definitions in the service framework let you set timeouts, logging and a circuit breaker, so one slow service doesn't stall checkout.
whyWrong: Tax is needed during checkout, not overnight.
No timeout lets the call hang and block the shopper.
Calling from the browser exposes the integration and is hard to secure.

sampleQuestions.question: A new site is being built from scratch with a headless front end. Which API set should be the default choice?
options: SOAP web services
OCAPI, the earlier generation of the APIs
SCAPI and the Shopper APIs
Direct access to the database
sampleQuestions.explanation: SCAPI is the current API set for headless builds and is where Salesforce is investing.
whyWrong: SOAP isn't the storefront API for B2C Commerce.
OCAPI still works but is the older choice for new builds.
There is no direct database access on the platform.

sampleQuestions.question: Before Black Friday, a load test shows some pages breaking platform quotas. What should the team do?
options: Ask shoppers to visit at quieter times
Ignore it entirely, since quotas only ever apply in sandboxes
Turn off the eCDN
Fix the code that breaks the quotas before peak
sampleQuestions.explanation: Quotas are enforced on Production. Code that breaks them can fail under load, so it must be fixed before peak trading.
whyWrong: Asking shoppers to wait isn't a real fix.
Quotas apply in Production too.
Turning off the eCDN would make performance worse.

sampleQuestions.question: The merchandising team should manage promotions but must not change site code or payment settings. How is this controlled?
options: Business Manager roles with least privilege
Give everyone Administrator access
Remove the promotions module from Business Manager
Share one login for the whole team
sampleQuestions.explanation: Business Manager roles let you grant only the modules each team needs, such as promotions, without wider access.
whyWrong: Full admin access gives far more than the team needs.
Removing promotions stops the team doing their job.
Shared logins remove accountability and are a security risk.

sampleQuestions.question: Product images load slowly for shoppers in Asia, while the site is hosted in Europe. What helps most?
options: Move every one of the images into the cartridge
Serve images and static files via eCDN
Turn off page caching
Make all images larger
sampleQuestions.explanation: The eCDN serves static files from locations close to the shopper, which cuts load times far from the main site.
whyWrong: Images in cartridges still come from the same place and bloat code.
Page caching helps speed. Turning it off makes things worse.
Larger images load more slowly.

sampleQuestions.question: When should an architect choose SFRA over a headless storefront?
options: When the site won't use any Salesforce APIs
When the team has deep React skills and wants full control
When speed to market and standard commerce features matter most
When the brand needs a front end shared with a mobile app and kiosks
sampleQuestions.explanation: SFRA gives a working storefront with standard features out of the box, so it is often the faster route to launch.
whyWrong: Every B2C Commerce storefront relies on the platform either way.
Strong React teams wanting full control is the case for headless.
Sharing one front end across channels is a strength of headless, not SFRA.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer wants to show different home page banners per country without code changes. What should be used?
options: Hard-code banners in ISML templates
Separate cartridges per country
Content slots and assets in Business Manager
A custom object that holds raw HTML strings
sampleQuestions.explanation: Content slots and assets let merchandisers manage banners per site or locale in Business Manager without a deployment.
whyWrong: Hard-coded banners need a code change every time.
Separate cartridges per country add needless code.
HTML in custom objects is hard to manage and skips the content tools.
